summary: Provides shared terms and metrics for benchmarking sub-IP protection mechanisms, such as automatic protection switching, VRRP, stateful high availability and MPLS fast reroute. The results are measured at the IP layer. Other documents can use this vocabulary when they define test methods.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC supplies the words for testing equipment that keeps traffic running when part of a network fails. It names the parts of a protected network, the events that happen when something breaks, and the numbers a test reports. Because the measurements are taken at the IP layer, two different protection mechanisms can be compared on the same terms.

subtitle: The shared vocabulary for measuring how fast a network switches traffic to a backup route when something fails.

tldr.problem: Protection mechanisms that work below the IP layer need to be benchmarked with the same words and the same instants, so that a fast failover in one technology can be compared with another.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the general model of a protection benchmark, the path and node vocabulary, five kinds of protection, the switching events, five benchmarks and three ways of calculating failover time, all measured at the IP layer.
tldr.outcome: It is the companion to RFC 6412, which defines the vocabulary for IP-layer convergence, and it is intended as the common base for the methodology documents written for individual protection technologies.

facts.label: Minimum flows for per-flow assessment
facts.value: 16 flows spread over the routing table

today: RFC 6414 is an Informational document, and the metadata shows no obsoleting and no updating RFC. It was written as the common base for the per-technology protection benchmarking methodologies, and it builds on the IP-layer convergence terms defined in RFC 6412.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 6414 is the terminology document for benchmarking sub-IP protection mechanisms. The IP network layer provides route convergence to protect data traffic against planned and unplanned failures in the Internet, and fast convergence times are critical to maintaining reliable network connectivity and performance. Technologies that function at sub-IP layers can be enabled to give IP traffic further protection, by providing the failure recovery at the sub-IP layer so that the outage is not observed at the IP layer at all.

The sub-IP protection technologies the RFC names are High Availability (HA) stateful failover, Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP), Automatic Protection Switching (APS) for SONET/SDH, Resilient Packet Ring (RPR) for Ethernet, and Fast Reroute for Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS-FRR).

Benchmarking terminology for IP-layer convergence was defined in RFC 6412, but different terminology and methodologies are needed for sub-IP protection mechanisms. The metrics are measured at the IP layer, so the results are always in reference to IP and independent of the specific protection mechanism being used. The purpose of this document is to provide a single terminology for benchmarking sub-IP protection mechanisms, so that different implementations of one mechanism can be compared, and so that different mechanisms can be compared with each other. The terminology can be applied to methodologies that benchmark with a single stream of traffic or with multiple streams, and the traffic flow may be unidirectional or bidirectional as the methodology indicates.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC supplies the words for testing equipment that keeps traffic running when part of a network fails. The tests look at traffic at the IP layer, so two different protection mechanisms can be compared on the same terms.

sections.title: The General Model
sections.content:
The RFC gives the sequence of events a protection benchmark measures. A Failover Event is when the Primary Path fails. Failure Detection is when that Failover Event is detected. Failover is when the Backup Path becomes the Working Path because of the Failover Event. Restoration is when the Primary Path recovers from the Failover Event. Reversion is optional, and is when the Primary Path becomes the Working Path again.

A benchmark must use a Protection-Switching System that consists of at least two Protection-Switching Nodes, an ingress node known as the Headend Node and an egress node known as the Merge Node. The system must include either a Primary Path and a Backup Path, or a Primary Node and a Standby Node. A Failover Event occurs along the Primary Path or at the Primary Node. The Working Path is the Primary Path before the Failover Event and the Backup Path after it. A Tester is set outside the two paths or nodes, as it sends and receives IP traffic along the Working Path. The Tester must record the IP packet sequence numbers, the departure time and the arrival time, so that Failover Time, Additive Latency, Packet Reordering, Duplicate Packets and Reversion Time can be measured. The Tester may be a single device or a test system.

Five models may be used. Link Protection covers a Failover Event on the link between two nodes along the Primary Path. Node Protection covers a Failover Event at a node along the Primary Path. Path Protection covers link or node failures for multiple hops along the Primary Path. Local Link Protection protects a link between two nodes without using a Backup Node, an example being SONET APS. High Availability Protection protects a Primary Node with a redundant Standby Node, with State Control provided between the two nodes; failure of the Primary Node is detected at the sub-IP layer to force traffic to switch to the Standby Node, which has state maintained for zero or minimal packet loss.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC fixes the order of events a test measures: something fails, the equipment notices, traffic moves to the backup route, the original route comes back, and traffic may then move back to it. The test equipment sits outside the network and records packet numbers and arrival times.

sections.title: Paths and Kinds of Protection
sections.content:
A Path is a unidirectional sequence of nodes and links in the sub-IP layer: an ingress node that forwards IP packets into the DUT or SUT, nodes in between that forward data frames using sub-IP information, and an egress node that outputs sub-IP frames as IP packets. A path is unidirectional, so the reverse direction is a separate path, and a bidirectional path is benchmarked as two independent unidirectional paths. Examples are the SONET/SDH path and the label switched path for MPLS.

Three path roles matter for protection. The Working Path is the path the DUT or SUT is currently using to forward packets. The Primary Path is the preferred point-to-point path, and it is the Working Path before a Failover Event. A Protected Primary Path is a Primary Path that has a Backup Path, and it must include at least one Protection-Switching Node. The Backup Path exists to carry data traffic only if a Failover Event occurs on a Primary Path; it must be created before the Failover Event, and it may be a Standby Backup Path established beforehand or a Dynamic Backup Path established when the event occurs. Backup Paths come in dedicated recovery forms, 1+1 or 1:1, shared 1:N, and associated shared M:N.

Two further terms describe how paths relate to each other. Disjoint Paths are a pair of paths that share no common link or node other than the ingress and egress. The Point of Local Repair (PLR) is a node along the Primary Path that can perform Failover and is also the ingress node for a Backup Path protecting another node or link; there may be several PLRs along a Primary Path, and the PLR can be any node on it except the egress node. A Shared Risk Link Group (SRLG) is a set of links that share the same physical or logical risk, and the group fails as a whole when the shared resource fails.

Five kinds of protection build on those paths. Link Protection signals a Backup Path to at least one Backup Node to protect against failure of interfaces and links along a Primary Path. Node Protection signals a Backup Path to protect against failure of interfaces, links and nodes, and it also provides Link Protection. Path Protection signals a Backup Path to provide protection along the entire Primary Path, covering every node and link on it. Local Link Protection is a Backup Path that is a redundant path between two nodes and does not use a Backup Node, as provided by systems such as SONET APS. Redundant Node Protection is a Protection-Switching System with a Primary Node protected by a Standby Node along the Primary Path, as provided by VRRP and HA; the failover may be stateful, with state exchanged in-band or over an out-of-band State Control Interface, and the Standby Node may be active or passive. The Backup Span is the number of hops used by a Backup Path, obtained by counting the nodes along it.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC names the parts: the route traffic normally takes, the standby route, the node that decides to switch, and the kinds of protection built from those. It also names the group of links that share one physical or logical risk, so two routes that look independent can be recognised as likely to fail together.

sections.title: Protection Switching Events
sections.content:
A Protection-Switching System is a DUT or SUT that is capable of Failure Detection and Failover from a Primary Path to a Backup Path or Standby Node when a Failover Event occurs. It includes the mechanisms for both Failure Detection and Failover.

A Failover Event is a planned or unplanned action in the network that results in a change in the path that data traffic traverses, such as link failure or router failure. Routing changes are Convergence Events in the sense of RFC 6412 and are not Failover Events, which keeps Failover Events at sub-IP layers. Failover may take place at the PLR or at the ingress, and when it is at the ingress it is generally on a path disjoint from the ingress to the egress.

Failure Detection is the process of identifying at a sub-IP layer a Failover Event at a Primary Node or along the Primary Path. It happens at the Primary Node or the ingress node of the Primary Path, using a sub-IP mechanism such as detection of a link down event or a timeout for receipt of a control packet. A failure may be completely isolated, may affect a set of links that share a single SRLG such as a port with many sub-interfaces, or may affect multiple links that are not part of an SRLG.

Failover is the process of switching data traffic from the protected Primary Path to the Backup Path once the failure has been detected. Failover to a Backup Path provides Link Protection, Node Protection or Path Protection. Failover is complete when Packet Loss, Out-of-order Packets and Duplicate Packets are no longer observed; Forwarding Delay may continue to be observed.

Restoration is the state in which the Primary Path has recovered from the Failover Event but is not yet forwarding packets, because the Backup Path remains the Working Path. Reversion is the state in which the Primary Path has become the Working Path and is forwarding packets again. A Protection-Switching System may or may not support Reversion, and if it does, Reversion must occur after Restoration. A potential problem with Reversion is the discontinuity in end-to-end delay when the Forwarding Delays along the Primary Path and the Backup Path differ, which can cause Out-of-order Packets, Duplicate Packets and increased Jitter.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC separates the moment the network changes from the moment the equipment reacts. A change caused by a link or router failure is a failover event; a routing change is not. Detection happens at the primary node or at the ingress, and the switch to the backup counts as finished only once no packets are lost, reordered or duplicated.

sections.title: Benchmarks and Failover Time Methods
sections.content:
Five benchmarks are defined. Failover Packet Loss is the amount of packet loss produced by a Failover Event until Failover completes; the measurement begins when the last unimpaired packet is received by the Tester on the Protected Primary Path and ends when the first unimpaired packet is received on the Backup Path. It includes packets that were lost, reordered or delayed, and it may reach 100% of the offered load. Reversion Packet Loss is the same measurement taken across the return to the Primary Path. Failover Time is the amount of time it takes for Failover to complete successfully, and Reversion Time is the amount of time it takes for Reversion to complete so that the Primary Path is restored as the Working Path. Both are measured in milliseconds. Additive Backup Delay is the increased Forwarding Delay that results from traffic traversing the Backup Path instead of the Primary Path, computed as the Forwarding Delay on the Backup Path minus the Forwarding Delay on the Primary Path. It may be a negative result, which is theoretically possible but could be indicative of a sub-optimum network configuration.

Three methods calculate Failover Time and Reversion Time, and the RFC recommends the Timestamp-Based Method (TBM). The Time-Based Loss Method (TBLM) uses a time scale on the Tester to measure the interval of Failover Packet Loss, indicated by the duration of non-zero packet loss; it includes failure detection time and the time for data traffic to begin traversing the Backup Path, and it is calculated as Time(Failover) minus Time(Failover Event). The Packet-Loss-Based Method (PLBM) takes the number of packets lost, divides it by the Offered Load rate and multiplies by 1000 to obtain milliseconds; if traffic is sent to more than one destination, it gives the average loss over the measured destinations. The Timestamp-Based Method (TBM) uses the timestamp in the packet payload, rather than the Tester clock, to quantify the interval between unimpaired packets arriving in the test stream. An unimpaired packet is one that is not lost, reordered or duplicated, and it may be detected by checking that a sequence number in the payload equals the next expected number; a sequence gap or a sequence reversal indicates impaired packets.

The methods may be assessed on a per-flow basis using at least 16 flows spread over the routing table, and using more flows is better. Otherwise a prefix-dependency in the implementation of a particular protection technology could be missed. The test designer must be aware of the number of packets per second sent to each prefix, because that sets the sampling of the path and the time resolution for measuring Failover Time on a per-flow basis.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC reports how many packets were lost and how long the switch took, in milliseconds. Three ways of timing it are offered, and the RFC recommends the one that reads the timestamp inside each packet, because that measures the gap between good packets as the network user sees it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Benchmarking activities as described in this memo are limited to technology characterization using controlled stimuli in a laboratory environment, with dedicated address space. The benchmarking network topology must be an independent test setup and must not be connected to devices that may forward the test traffic into a production network or misroute traffic to the test management network.

Benchmarking is performed on a black-box basis, relying solely on measurements observable external to the DUT or SUT. Special capabilities should not exist in the DUT or SUT specifically for benchmarking purposes, so that any security implications arising from the device should be identical in the lab and in production networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Run the tests on a separate network with its own address space, and do not connect that network to production equipment. Measure only what an outside observer can see, and do not add benchmarking-only features to the equipment under test.

viz.caption: THE FIVE KINDS OF PROTECTION IN RFC 6414

items.title: Link Protection
items.text: A Backup Path protects against failure of interfaces and links along the Primary Path.

items.title: Node Protection
items.text: A Backup Path protects against failure of interfaces, links and nodes, and also gives Link Protection.

items.title: Path Protection
items.text: A Backup Path protects the entire Primary Path, covering every node and link on it.

items.title: Local Link Protection
items.text: A redundant path between two nodes that uses no Backup Node, as in SONET APS.

items.title: Redundant Node Protection
items.text: A Primary Node protected by a Standby Node, as in VRRP and HA.
